name: Refugee Status Under the Refugees Act 1998

requirements.blocker_text: The Refugees Act 1998 is Tanzania's principal domestic refugee legislation, applied alongside Tanzania's ratification of the 1951 Refugee Convention, its 1967 Protocol, and the 1969 OAU Refugee Convention, in collaboration with UNHCR. As of 2018, Tanzania withdrew from the Comprehensive Refugee Response Framework and restricted refugees to living in designated camps (primarily Nyarugusu and Nduta in Kigoma region, holding roughly 83% of the refugee population), with refugees barred from working, trading, or gardening inside camps.

outcome.duration_length: indefinite pending durable solution (repatriation, resettlement, or naturalization)
outcome.physical_presence_requirement: confined to designated refugee camps/settlements absent special permission

sources.title: Permanent Mission of the United Republic of Tanzania to the UN, Geneva -- confirms the Refugees Act 1998 as principal national legislation, Tanzania's status as party to the 1951 Convention/1967 Protocol/1969 OAU Convention, roughly 241,883 refugees and asylum-seekers as of March 2024 (mostly Burundian and Congolese, ~83% in two Kigoma-region camps), and the historic naturalization of 162,000 Burundian refugees

notes: NEW COUNTRY BUILD (Tanzania). STATUS: DRAFT -- the tier-1 mission source confirms the Refugees Act 1998 exists and gives population/policy context, but does not detail the actual refugee-status-determination procedure (who decides, appeal rights, timelines), so the specific determination mechanism is not independently sourced in this build. LIVE POLICY-REVERSAL FINDING, WORTH LEADING WITH: Tanzania was long celebrated as unusually generous toward refugees, including a widely-reported HISTORIC decision naturalizing roughly 162,000 Burundian refugees (largely from the 1972 exodus) -- but this is a closed, one-off historical program, not a standing route a current refugee can invoke, and policy has moved sharply the other way since: Tanzania withdrew from the Comprehensive Refugee Response Framework in 2018, banned camp-based work/trade/gardening, and -- per Human Rights Watch, Foreign Policy, and a February 2026 UN News report all reviewed in this build (tier 3/4, not this route's cited source but corroborating context) -- has pressured over 145,000 Burundian refugees to return since 2017 through means advocacy groups describe as coercive, including a 2019 presidential directive telling refugees not to 'expect citizenship while Burundi is now stable.' As of the UN News report reviewed (February 2026), concerns about coercive repatriation from Tanzania remain active and current, not merely historical. This is a sharper and more recent open-door-to-restriction reversal than Somalia's fragmentation or Tunisia's asylum-suspension crisis noted elsewhere in this dataset, and should be foregrounded rather than treated as a minor caveat. family_can_work left null since dependents' work rights specifically within camps were not detailed beyond the general camp work ban.
